## Storage & RWX (decision-critical)

Che does **not** require RWX. The default is `per-user` ("a single PVC for all
workspaces created by a user"); `per-workspace` gives "each workspace its own PVC";
`ephemeral` is non-persistent [8]. With RWO, "Starting another, concurrently running
workspace with a `ReadWriteOnce` PV might fail" [9] — so on Longhorn RWO the safe
choices are **per-workspace** (one RWO PVC per workspace pod) or ephemeral. The legacy
"Che needs RWX" reputation came from the old `common` strategy on multi-node clusters,
now superseded by `per-user` as default [8]. RWX is not required.

## The TLS / OIDC clash with the HTTP-only TS Operator (decision-critical)

Che's gateway and auth assume TLS end-to-end: "Che components communications with
external services are encrypted with TLS and require TLS certificates signed by
trusted CAs" [12], and an OIDC provider (typically Keycloak) is mandatory on vanilla
k8s — issue #21107 confirms only a flag to *skip the provider health check*, not to
remove auth [11]. The operator runs the TS Operator with **tailnet HTTPS deliberately
disabled** (HTTP only); Tailscale Ingress is HTTPS-only anyway [42]. Running Che's
OIDC/OAuth-proxy flow purely over HTTP behind Tailscale is unverified and a likely
hard blocker — this, plus weight, is Che's core misfit.

## Weight

Control-plane limits total ~13 GiB memory / 8.4 CPU before any workspace (gateway 5.3
GiB, DevWorkspace Controller 5 GiB) [10]; requests are modest (~1.2 GiB / 1.2 CPU) so
it *fits* on 3 nodes, but the operator + DevWorkspace-operator + gateway + dashboard +
registries is heavy to run for one person.

## Counter-evidence

Heavy vanilla-k8s prerequisites (Keycloak + cert-manager + OIDC), known install
fragility off OpenShift, a postStart + Che-Code bug [13], and TLS-everywhere
assumptions all point away from a single-operator HTTP-only homelab. No abandonment —
the project is active [7].
